questions.q: A school nurse writes four questions in her notebook: (i) What is Ravi's weight today? (ii) How heavy are the schoolbags that Class 7 students carry? (iii) How many hours do the students of our school sleep on a school night? (iv) How many days are there in the month of June? (a) Sort the four into statistical and non-statistical questions, giving a reason for each group. (b) For question (iii), she asks 8 students and gets 8, 7, 9, 6, 8, 7, 8 and 9 hours. Write one statistical statement that uses a number you calculate from this data. (c) Ravi reads her notes and says, 'So every student in our school sleeps 7.75 hours.' Is Ravi right? Give a reason from the data.
questions.a: (a) (ii) and (iii) are statistical: the answers vary from student to student, so data must be collected. (i) and (iv) are not: each has one fixed answer (Ravi's weight today; 30 days). (b) Total = 8 + 7 + 9 + 6 + 8 + 7 + 8 + 9 = 62 hours; mean = 62 / 8 = 7.75 hours, so a statement such as 'These 8 students sleep 7.75 hours a night on average.' (c) No. 7.75 is an average of 8 students only; the values themselves vary from 6 to 9 and no student slept exactly 7.75 hours, so an average does not describe every individual, nor the whole school from 8 students.
s: (a) names (ii) and (iii) as statistical because the answers vary and need data, and (i) and (iv) as non-statistical because each has a single fixed answer
(b) finds total 62 and mean 62 / 8 = 7.75 hours and writes it as a statement about these students on average
(c) says Ravi is wrong because an average does not describe each student: the values vary from 6 to 9 and none is 7.75
(c) adds that 8 students are only a few of the school, so their average cannot be claimed for every student of the school

questions.q: In a summer reading drive, Group Tagore (4 students) read a mean of 9 books per student. When Group Kalam (6 students) is included, the mean for all 10 students is 7.2 books. (a) Find the total number of books read by all 10 students and by Group Tagore. (b) Find the mean number of books per student in Group Kalam. (c) Rahul says, 'The combined mean 7.2 is 1.8 below Tagore's 9, so Kalam's mean must be 1.8 below 7.2, that is 5.4.' Explain what is wrong with his reasoning, using your answer to (b). (d) Kalam's leader claims that every student in her group read at least 7 books. Show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: (a) All 10: 10 x 7.2 = 72 books. Tagore: 4 x 9 = 36 books. (b) Kalam's total = 72 - 36 = 36 books, so its mean = 36 / 6 = 6 books. (c) Rahul treats the combined mean as lying midway between the two group means, which happens only when the groups are the same size. Kalam has more students (6 against 4), so its mean counts more and the combined mean lies nearer to Kalam's: 7.2 is 1.2 above 6 but 1.8 below 9. Kalam's mean is 6, not 5.4. (d) If each of the 6 students read at least 7 books, Kalam would have read at least 6 x 7 = 42 books, but its total is only 36. So at least one Kalam student read fewer than 7 books.
s: (a) finds the combined total 10 x 7.2 = 72 and Tagore's total 4 x 9 = 36
(b) finds Kalam's total 72 - 36 = 36 and mean 36 / 6 = 6
(c) explains that the combined mean is midway only for equal-sized groups; Kalam is larger, so 7.2 lies nearer its mean (1.2 from 6, 1.8 from 9)
(d) shows at least 6 x 7 = 42 books would be needed but Kalam read only 36, so the claim is false

questions.q: Seven members of a cycling club rode these distances (km) on a Sunday: 18, 24, 15, 30, 21, 27 and 12. (a) Find the mean distance. (b) An eighth member joins the ride and, with her distance included, the mean for all 8 becomes 22 km. How far did she ride? (c) Forget the eighth member. The club secretary finds that the rider recorded as 12 km had actually ridden 26 km. Without adding the seven values again, find the corrected mean of the seven riders and show how you got it.
questions.a: (a) Total = 18 + 24 + 15 + 30 + 21 + 27 + 12 = 147 km; mean = 147 / 7 = 21 km. (b) Total for 8 = 8 x 22 = 176 km, so she rode 176 - 147 = 29 km. (c) The total rises by 26 - 12 = 14 km; shared among 7 riders the mean rises by 14 / 7 = 2 km, so the corrected mean is 21 + 2 = 23 km (check: 161 / 7 = 23).
s: (a) finds total 147 km and mean 147 / 7 = 21 km
(b) finds the new total 8 x 22 = 176 km
(b) finds her distance 176 - 147 = 29 km
(c) uses the change 14 km shared by 7 to raise the mean by 2, giving 23 km

questions.q: The minutes by which two school buses arrived late at school over the same 10 days were recorded. Route 1: 4, 6, 5, 5, 7, 4, 6, 5, 6, 2. Route 2: 0, 12, 1, 9, 0, 14, 2, 1, 10, 1. (a) Find the mean delay of each route. (b) Find the range of each route. (c) The transport in-charge says, 'Both routes have the same mean delay, so they are equally dependable.' Do you agree? Use your answers to (a) and (b), and say how the dots of the two routes would look on a dot plot. (d) Looking only at a dot plot of Route 2, can a parent tell on which day the 14-minute delay happened? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Route 1 total = 50, mean 50 / 10 = 5 minutes; Route 2 total = 50, mean 50 / 10 = 5 minutes. (b) Route 1 range = 7 - 2 = 5 minutes; Route 2 range = 14 - 0 = 14 minutes. (c) Disagree. The means are equal, but Route 2's range (14) is much larger than Route 1's (5): on a dot plot Route 1's dots cluster between 2 and 7, while Route 2's spread from 0 to 14, so Route 2 is far less predictable and Route 1 is more dependable. (d) No. A dot plot sorts the values and loses the original day-wise order, so it shows that one delay was 14 minutes but not which day.
s: (a) finds both totals 50 and both means 5 minutes
(b) finds the ranges 5 (7 - 2) and 14 (14 - 0)
(c) disagrees: the means are equal but Route 2's range 14 is far larger than Route 1's 5, so Route 1 is more dependable
(c) describes Route 1's dots clustered from 2 to 7 and Route 2's spread from 0 to 14, and (d) says no, because a dot plot loses the original day-wise order

questions.q: A ration-shop clerk noted the waiting times (minutes) of 8 customers one morning: 6, 9, 4, 7, 5, 8, 6 and one more value that was smudged. She remembers that the mean waiting time was 12 minutes; the long wait happened when the weighing machine broke down. (a) Find the smudged waiting time. (b) Find the median waiting time of all 8 customers. (c) Name the outlier and find the median and the mean of the other 7 values (mean to two decimal places). (d) Which measure changed more when the outlier was removed? Explain why, using what the outlier does to the total.
questions.a: (a) Total of 8 = 8 x 12 = 96; the seven known values add to 45, so the smudged value = 96 - 45 = 51 minutes. (b) Sorted: 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 51; the two middle values are 6 and 7, so median = (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5 minutes. (c) The outlier is 51. Without it: 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9; median = 6 minutes; total = 45, mean = 45 / 7 = 6.43 minutes. (d) The mean changed more (12 to 6.43, a fall of about 5.57) than the median (6.5 to 6, a fall of 0.5). The 51 adds a lot to the total, which is shared over all values, so it pulls the mean up; the median depends only on the middle position, so it hardly moves.
s: (a) finds the total 8 x 12 = 96 and the missing value 96 - 45 = 51
(b) sorts the data and takes the average of the two middle values, (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5
(c) names 51 as the outlier and finds median 6 and mean 45 / 7 = 6.43 for the other 7
(d) says the mean changed more and explains that the outlier enlarges the total that the mean depends on, while the median depends only on the middle value(s)

questions.q: Make up the scores (whole numbers, out of 20) of 6 students in a spelling test so that all three conditions hold: the median is 12, the mean is 10, and exactly one score is an outlier at the lower end (many answers are possible). (a) Write your 6 scores in order. (b) Show that the median is 12. (c) Show that the mean is 10. (d) Say which score is the outlier and explain why the mean of your data is less than its median.
questions.a: One possible set: (a) 0, 11, 12, 12, 12, 13. (b) The two middle values (3rd and 4th) are 12 and 12, so median = (12 + 12) / 2 = 12. (c) Total = 0 + 11 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 13 = 60, mean = 60 / 6 = 10. (d) 0 is the outlier: it is far below the other scores, which lie between 11 and 13. A low outlier makes the total smaller and pulls the mean down towards it, while the middle values stay at 12, so mean 10 < median 12. (Any set of 6 whole numbers from 0 to 20 with total 60, middle two values averaging 12 and exactly one value far below the rest earns full marks. Reject a set with two low values, or with no value clearly far from the rest, for part (d).)
s: (a) lists six whole numbers from 0 to 20 in increasing order
(b) shows the two middle values average to 12
(c) shows the total is 60, so the mean is 60 / 6 = 10
(d) names exactly one low value far from the rest as the outlier and says it pulls the mean below the median

questions.q: In an inter-house quiz, the points scored in 7 rounds were recorded. Asha: 8, 0, 6, did not take part, 10, 0, 9. Babu: 7, 6, 7, 5, 6, 7, 4. (a) Find Asha's mean score per round and say what number you divided by, and why. (b) Find Asha's median and Babu's mean and median. (c) The captain says, 'Asha is the better scorer, because her median is higher than Babu's.' Give one reason that supports the captain and one reason against, using the mean and the median of each player.
questions.a: (a) Asha played 6 rounds (the round she did not take part in is not counted, but her two 0s are): total = 8 + 0 + 6 + 10 + 0 + 9 = 33, mean = 33 / 6 = 5.5. (b) Asha sorted: 0, 0, 6, 8, 9, 10, median = (6 + 8) / 2 = 7. Babu total = 42, mean = 42 / 7 = 6; sorted 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, median 6. (c) For: Asha's median 7 is above Babu's 6, and in half her rounds she scored 8 or more, higher than Babu's best of 7. Against: her two zeros are low values that pull her mean (5.5) below her median and below Babu's mean (6); Babu never scored below 4, so he is more consistent and scores more per round on average.
s: (a) divides 33 by 6, explaining that the round not played is left out while the 0s are counted, mean 5.5
(b) finds Asha's median (6 + 8) / 2 = 7
(b) finds Babu's mean 42 / 7 = 6 and median 6
(c) gives one reason for (Asha's median 7 is above Babu's 6, or she scored 8 or more in three rounds) and one against (her two zeros pull her mean 5.5 below Babu's mean 6)

questions.q: The waste paper (kg) collected for recycling by Class 6 and Class 7 in four months was: June: Class 6 48, Class 7 36; July: Class 6 60, Class 7 72; August: Class 6 84, Class 7 66; September: Class 6 30, Class 7 54. Meera draws a double bar graph with the scale 1 unit = 12 kg. (a) How long are the two bars for July? (b) In which month is the difference between the two classes the largest? Give the difference in kg and in units. (c) Meera draws Class 7's August bar 6.5 units long. Is she right? Show the correct length. (d) Her friend suggests 1 unit = 5 kg instead, but the graph paper is only 10 units tall. Show whether this scale would work.
questions.a: (a) July: Class 6 60 / 12 = 5 units, Class 7 72 / 12 = 6 units. (b) Differences: June 12 kg, July 12 kg, August 18 kg, September 24 kg; the largest is September, 24 kg = 24 / 12 = 2 units. (c) No: 66 / 12 = 5.5 units, so her bar is 1 unit (12 kg) too long. (d) The tallest bar, Class 6 in August, would be 84 / 5 = 16.8 units, more than 10 units, so it would not fit; 1 unit = 12 kg (tallest bar 7 units) works.
s: (a) finds 60 / 12 = 5 units and 72 / 12 = 6 units
(b) finds the four differences and picks September, 24 kg = 2 units
(c) shows 66 / 12 = 5.5 units, so 6.5 is wrong
(d) finds the tallest bar 84 / 5 = 16.8 units, more than 10, so the scale does not fit

questions.q: A school's record gives the average weights (kg) of children. Age 9: boys 28.0, girls 27.6. Age 10: boys 31.0, girls 31.2. Age 11: boys 34.2, girls 35.5. Age 12: boys 37.6, girls 40.1. Age 13: boys 42.0, girls 44.0. (a) Between which two successive ages did the average boy gain the most weight, and between which two did the average girl gain the most? Give the gains. (b) Find how much heavier the average girl was than the average boy at each age. Is the statement 'The gap between girls and boys widened at every step from age 9 to age 13' justified? (c) The school has 300 twelve-year-old boys and 100 twelve-year-old girls. Sunil says, 'The average weight of all 400 twelve-year-olds is (37.6 + 40.1) / 2 = 38.85 kg.' Is he right? Find the correct average. (d) Is the statement 'From age 9 to age 13, the average girl gained more weight than the average boy' justified? Show the comparison.
questions.a: (a) Boys' gains: 9 to 10: 3.0, 10 to 11: 3.2, 11 to 12: 3.4, 12 to 13: 4.4 kg, so boys gained most between 12 and 13 (4.4 kg). Girls' gains: 3.6, 4.3, 4.6, 3.9 kg, so girls gained most between 11 and 12 (4.6 kg). (b) Girls minus boys: age 9: -0.4 (boys heavier by 0.4), age 10: 0.2, age 11: 1.3, age 12: 2.5, age 13: 2.0 kg. Not justified: the gap grew up to age 12 but narrowed from 2.5 to 2.0 kg between 12 and 13. (c) No. Taking the middle of the two averages is fair only when the two groups are the same size; here there are three times as many boys. Total = 300 x 37.6 + 100 x 40.1 = 11280 + 4010 = 15290 kg, so the average = 15290 / 400 = 38.225 kg (about 38.2 kg), nearer the boys' 37.6. (d) Justified: girls gained 44.0 - 27.6 = 16.4 kg and boys 42.0 - 28.0 = 14.0 kg, so the average girl gained 2.4 kg more. (This is about averages only, not every girl and boy.)
s: (a) finds the successive gains and names boys 12 to 13 (4.4 kg) and girls 11 to 12 (4.6 kg)
(b) finds the gaps -0.4, 0.2, 1.3, 2.5, 2.0 and says not justified because the gap narrowed from 2.5 to 2.0 between 12 and 13
(c) says Sunil is wrong because the groups are of unequal size, and finds 15290 / 400 = 38.225 kg (about 38.2 kg)
(d) compares 16.4 kg with 14.0 kg and says justified
